meta.location: Mulek, Bountiful, and the borders by the east sea
principles: A commander who knows what he cannot do

world_behind.title: The Lamanites wake to a dead king
world_behind.text: Verse 1 has them find Amalickiah dead in his tent and Teancum ready for battle. They abandon the northward march and shut themselves in Mulek.

world_behind.title: Ammoron inherits and holds
world_behind.text: Verse 3 makes the brother king; verse 4 has him order the captured cities kept, because they had cost so much blood.

world_behind.title: Teancum declines the attack twice
world_behind.text: Verses 5 and 17 have him look at the fortifications, judge it impossible, and stop. Mormon records the refusal as sound judgment.

world_behind.title: Moroni's orders arrive by letter
world_behind.text: Verses 8 through 11 give five instructions, covering prisoners, the fortifying of Bountiful, the narrow pass, harassment, and stratagem where a city can be retaken.

world_behind.title: Prisoners are held as currency
world_behind.text: Verse 8 says to keep every Lamanite prisoner as a ransom for Nephites taken. Alma 54 and 55 are the negotiation this sets up.

world_behind.title: The Lamanites are fighting on two fronts by design
world_behind.text: Verses 12 and 13 have Ammoron open a western attack as a pull, leaving the eastern garrisons to wear down what stays behind.

world_behind.title: The council of war precedes the plan
world_behind.text: Verse 19 has Moroni, Teancum, and many chief captains meet to work out how to draw the Lamanites out. The decoy is a decision taken together.

words.text: Vastness, great size. The word occurs twice in this record and never in the King James Bible, both in these war chapters. Mormon uses it of the Lamanite numbers, as one of the two reasons Teancum did not attack.
A price paid to free a captive. It appears once in the record, and thirteen times in the King James Bible, where it usually names what redeems a life. Moroni uses it of prisoners held for exchange.
To wear down by repeated attack. Four uses here, none in the King James Bible, three of them inside these two chapters. Both sides use the method, and Mormon uses the word of both.
A formal meeting to decide. The phrase council of war occurs once in scripture. Mormon names Moroni, Teancum, and many chief captains, which makes the decoy a decision of the whole command.

Something used to lure an enemy out of position. The word turns up twice here, and never in the King James Bible. Mormon uses it here and again in Alma 58, both times of Nephite commanders drawing Lamanites out of forts.
Force, energy. Its count is three here and none in the King James Bible. Mormon applies it to the Lamanite pursuit, the moment the plan is working.

phrases.term: They found Amalickiah was dead in his own tent
phrases.text: The discovery, given from the Lamanite side. Alma 51 ended with Teancum's return; this verse shows the morning, and verse 2 gives the effect: the northward design abandoned.

phrases.term: They had not taken any cities save they had lost much blood
phrases.text: Ammoron's reason for holding what his brother took. The cost already paid becomes the argument for paying more, and it fixes the Lamanite posture for ten chapters.

phrases.term: Teancum thought it was not expedient that he should attempt to attack them in their forts
phrases.text: A commander declining a fight he cannot win. Mormon gives both reasons, the enemy's determination and their numbers, and treats the decision as sound.

phrases.term: He kept his men round about, as if making preparations for war; yea, and truly he was preparing
phrases.text: Mormon corrects the appearance in the same sentence. What looked like a feint was also real work, and the ambiguity is exactly what the position required.

phrases.term: That he should retain all the prisoners of the Lamanites as a ransom
phrases.text: Moroni turns captives into a negotiating position. The instruction is given before any exchange is proposed, and Alma 54 shows it being used.

phrases.term: Secure the narrow pass which led into the land northward
phrases.text: The chokepoint of Alma 50 becomes a standing military objective. Moroni's reason is that losing it would let the Lamanites harass on every side.

phrases.term: That perhaps he might take again by stratagem or some other way those cities
phrases.text: Moroni's own word for the method. He authorizes trickery in an order, which is what verses 21 through 26 then carry out.

phrases.term: I would come unto you, but behold, the Lamanites are upon us in the borders of the land by the west sea
phrases.text: The one line of Moroni's letter Mormon quotes directly. It explains the two-front problem from the Nephite side in a sentence.

phrases.term: That they might by some means flatter them out of their strongholds
phrases.text: The council's stated aim. Flatter here means entice, and the word carries the same sense the record uses of Amalickiah, applied now to a tactic instead of a man.

phrases.term: Moroni, having no hopes of meeting them upon fair grounds
phrases.text: Mormon explains why the decoy was chosen. Jacob refused the open field, so the plan follows a refused invitation to fight on even terms.

phrases.term: They took courage and pursued them with vigor
phrases.text: The Lamanites do the one thing the plan needs. Mormon reports their confidence at the moment it becomes the mechanism of their loss.

verses.label: v. 1
verses.title: A date fixed to a discovery
verses.text: The chapter opens on a calendar detail that nothing in the plot requires: "when the Lamanites awoke on the first morning of the first month, behold, they found Amalickiah was dead in his own tent." The previous chapter ended with the killing; this one starts with the finding, and the record chooses to date the finding rather than the deed. The same verse adds that Teancum "was ready to give them battle on that day," so the army wakes to a corpse and a line of soldiers in the same sentence.

verses.label: v. 3
verses.title: The same fact stated twice in one verse
verses.text: The succession is reported, then reported again with the terms reversed: "the brother of Amalickiah was appointed king over the people; and his name was Ammoron; thus king Ammoron, the brother of king Amalickiah, was appointed to reign." Relation, then name, then name and relation together. The record used the same order for Amalickiah himself at Alma 47:3, where the man was described before he was named. Here the doubling has a function the first one did not, since the reader needs to carry the new name forward for ten chapters.

verses.label: v. 4
verses.title: The record concedes the enemy's cost
verses.text: Ammoron's order to hold the captured cities comes with a clause the narrative does not need: "which they had taken by the shedding of blood; for they had not taken any cities save they had lost much blood." This is a war record written by the losing side of that campaign, and it stops to say the winners paid heavily. Nothing follows from the concession. No Nephite advantage is drawn from it, and the next verse returns to Teancum's preparations.

verses.label: v. 19–21
verses.title: The invitation before the trick
verses.text: The council of war does not open with a plan. Verse 20 has them send embassies asking the enemy commander "that he would come out with his armies to meet them upon the plains between the two cities," and reports the refusal in the same verse. Only then does verse 21 give the reason for what follows: "Moroni, having no hopes of meeting them upon fair grounds, therefore, he resolved upon a plan that he might decoy the Lamanites out of their strongholds." The record supplies the failed honest attempt as the justification for the deception, and puts them in that order.

verses.label: v. 25–39
verses.title: A chapter that ends up being about handing things over
verses.text: Weapons of war stands in six verses here, and five of the six are in the last nine verses. The phrase governs how the fighting stops each time: the city's defenders are killed only insofar as they "would not yield up their weapons of war" (v. 25), Moroni's order is to fall upon them "until they had given up their weapons" (v. 32), the rear ranks "delivered up their weapons of war" (v. 36), the chief captains "threw down their weapons of war at the feet of Moroni" (v. 38), and those who refused had them "taken from them" (v. 39). The battle is narrated as a sequence of surrenders rather than of casualties.

verses.label: v. 33
verses.title: Three appositives, and the middle one explains him
verses.text: The enemy commander is introduced with three clauses stacked together: "Jacob, being their leader, being also a Zoramite, and having an unconquerable spirit." The first is his office and the third is his character, and the second is the fact that makes the chapter's shape intelligible. The army defending a Lamanite city against Nephites is commanded by a Nephite dissenter, which is also why verse 20 could ask him for a fair field in the first place and expect to be understood.

verses.label: v. 40
verses.title: The chapter counts the living
verses.text: The last verse gives the only arithmetic in the chapter, and it is not a body count: "the number of prisoners who were taken exceeded more than the number of those who had been slain, yea, more than those who had been slain on both sides." Taken is used ten times in this chapter, which is more than in any other chapter of scripture, and the word does double duty throughout for cities seized and men captured. The closing sentence chooses the second meaning and makes the battle's result a population of prisoners.

chapter.title: Two commanders decline the same attack
chapter.text: Teancum in verse 5 and again in verse 17. Mormon records the refusals without criticism, and the chapter's solution is a plan instead of more force.

chapter.title: The orders are quoted as a list
chapter.text: Prisoners, Bountiful, the pass, harassment, stratagem, fortification. Mormon gives Moroni's letter as six concrete instructions and one apology for not coming.

chapter.title: Prisoners become policy before they become leverage
chapter.text: Verse 8 sets the rule; Alma 54 and 55 spend two chapters on the exchange it makes possible.

chapter.title: Both sides are trying to stretch the other
chapter.text: Ammoron opens a second front to draw Nephites west while his garrisons press east. Mormon states the intention plainly in verse 13.

chapter.title: The plan is made in committee
chapter.text: Verse 19 records a "council of war" with "Moroni and Teancum and many of the chief captains," and names its question, "what they should do to cause the Lamanites to come out against them to battle." Verse 20 reports the first attempt, an embassy inviting the enemy onto open ground, which fails. Only at verse 21, after both the meeting and the failed invitation, does the record say "he resolved upon a plan that he might decoy the Lamanites out of their strongholds." Two steps stand between the problem and the stratagem, and the first of them is a committee.

chapter.title: The enemy's courage is the mechanism
chapter.text: Verse 23 supplies the enemy's reasoning, "supposing by their numbers to overpower Teancum because of the smallness of his numbers," and their pursuit is what empties the city Moroni takes at verse 26. Verse 28 then records the moment they understand, "they fled in much confusion, lest perhaps they should not obtain the city Mulek before Lehi should overtake them." The decision that looked best to them at verse 23 is the one that loses them the city three verses later.

chapter.title: Freshness decides the second engagement
chapter.text: Verse 28 says the men of Lehi were fresh and the Lamanites wearied by their march. Mormon tracks the physical state of armies the way he tracks their armor.

chapter.title: The chapter ends in a surrender accepted
chapter.text: Hemmed in, they throw down their weapons and plead, and Moroni takes them prisoner. As in Alma 44, the fighting stops when the other side yields.

applications.title: Decline the attack you cannot win
applications.text: Teancum looked at the forts and stopped. When the direct approach is beyond your means, saying so is a decision rather than a failure.

applications.title: Hold what you will need to trade
applications.text: Moroni ordered prisoners kept before any exchange was on the table. Think ahead about what you may need to offer, and do not spend it early.

applications.title: Secure the chokepoint
applications.text: The narrow pass mattered more than its size. Identify the one place in your situation where losing control would cost you everything else, and hold it.

applications.title: Say plainly that you cannot come
applications.text: Moroni wrote that he would come to Teancum and then gave the reason he could not. When you are unable to help, the useful message names the willingness and the constraint together, so the other person can plan around your real answer.

applications.title: Decide it in council
applications.text: The plan came out of a meeting of captains. When you are stuck, put the problem in front of the people who know the ground, rather than working it out alone.

applications.title: Hold back so the other half can arrive
applications.text: Lehi was not desirous to overtake the fleeing Lamanites until they had met Moroni first. Restraint in the middle of a plan looks like inaction to everyone watching, so tell your people what the waiting is for.

applications.title: Offer terms the moment it turns
applications.text: Moroni saw the confusion and immediately offered to forbear shedding blood. When a conflict has visibly turned your way, that is the cheapest instant at which to end it, and making the offer costs you nothing.

applications.title: Count the ones who lived
applications.text: The chapter's closing tally is that the prisoners taken outnumbered all the dead on both sides. When you write up a hard episode, record what was saved with the same care you give to what was lost.

questions.text: What am I holding on to because of what it already cost me?
What have I been attacking head-on that I should stop attacking?
Where am I preparing in earnest while appearing to?
What have I had to say I cannot come to?
When did someone refuse me fair ground, and what did I do?
What have I pursued with vigor that was leading me away?
